title: Dataset overview and ticket volume
text: The analysis uses a stratified sample of 20000 tickets created between <PHONE> and <PHONE>. There are 8 categories and they are balanced: the largest is how_to with 12.7% of tickets and the smallest is bug with 12.3%. Ticket volume is flat over time at about 417 tickets per month. 50.6% of tickets are resolved and 39.2% are still open, in progress or on hold. Overall 42.1% of customers are negative. The ticket messages are built from only 96 unique sentences.

title: Ticket profile: priority, channel, product area, segment, platform, region, SLA
text: Share of tickets by field. priority: low 39.0%, medium 35.9%, high 19.9%, urgent 5.2%; channel: in_app 20.2%, email 20.2%, phone_transcript 19.9%, web_form 19.9%, chat 19.8%; product area: api_integration 14.7%, login_auth 14.7%, notifications 14.6%, billing 14.2%, data_export 14.1%, analytics_dashboard 14.0%, mobile_app 13.7%; customer segment: enterprise 20.6%, education 20.2%, non_profit 19.9%, small_business 19.8%, individual 19.5%; platform: android 20.2%, desktop_app 20.1%, web 20.0%, api_client 20.0%, ios 19.7%; region: MEA 20.5%, LATAM 20.3%, Unknown 20.0%, EU 19.8%, APAC 19.4%; sla plan: standard 60.4%, gold 29.3%, platinum 10.3%. Attachments are included in 25.0% of tickets. These fields do not tell the category apart: within every product area each category's share lies between 10.7% and 14.1%, so the classifiers use only the ticket description.

title: Customer satisfaction by category: which customers are unhappy
text: Customer sentiment and satisfaction (CSAT) differ a lot by category. Share of negative or very negative (unhappy, frustrated) customers and average CSAT per category, from worst to best: performance: 60.8% negative, CSAT 2.80; security_concern: 60.1% negative, CSAT 2.85; billing_problem: 59.1% negative, CSAT 2.82; account_access: 58.1% negative, CSAT 2.85; bug: 30.7% negative, CSAT 3.40; other: 29.0% negative, CSAT 3.45; feature_request: 20.0% negative, CSAT 3.73; how_to: 18.9% negative, CSAT 3.76. Problem categories make customers much unhappier than requests such as how_to and feature_request.

title: Resolution time: how long tickets take to resolve, reopen rate
text: Median resolution time of resolved tickets by priority: urgent: 4.0 hours; high: 12.7 hours; medium: 25.5 hours; low: 40.5 hours. By SLA plan: gold: 23.3 hours; platinum: 23.1 hours; standard: 23.0 hours. By category the median resolution time is almost the same everywhere: account_access: 22.4 hours; billing_problem: 23.3 hours; bug: 23.2 hours; feature_request: 23.3 hours; how_to: 23.7 hours; other: 23.6 hours; performance: 22.9 hours; security_concern: 22.6 hours. Priority drives how fast tickets are resolved, the category does not. The reopen rate is 5.1% overall; by priority: urgent: 5.1%; high: 5.1%; medium: 4.9%; low: 5.1%.

title: Routing: tickets per support queue and manual review
text: Predicted tickets per support queue with the TF-IDF model (low-confidence tickets go to Manual Triage): Manual Triage: 9141 tickets; Application Support (L2): 3299 tickets; Service Desk (L1): 2548 tickets; Product Management: 2497 tickets; Platform / SRE: 1684 tickets; Security Operations: 831 tickets. title: How good is the TF-IDF classifier: F1, precision, recall, accuracy
text: The original classifier is TF-IDF (1-2 grams) + Logistic Regression, evaluated with grouped 5-fold cross-validation by message (out-of-fold). Macro F1 is 0.541, weighted F1 0.541, macro precision 0.531, macro recall 0.584, accuracy 0.585 and macro ROC-AUC 0.862. Tickets with confidence below 60% go to manual review; that is 45.7% of tickets. The weakest categories are account_access, other, which have only 3 different sentences each, so the model rarely sees new wording for them. The BGE embedding model is better: macro F1 0.816.

title: TF-IDF model comparison: Logistic Regression vs SVM vs Naive Bayes
text: With TF-IDF features, on the held-out test messages the models scored: Majority baseline: macro F1 0.012, ROC-AUC 0.500; Naive Bayes: macro F1 0.611, ROC-AUC 0.915; Linear SVM: macro F1 0.611, ROC-AUC 0.886; Logistic Regression: macro F1 0.611, ROC-AUC 0.886. In grouped 5-fold cross-validation the macro F1 was: Majority baseline: 0.002; Naive Bayes: 0.591; Linear SVM: 0.591; Logistic Regression: 0.591. Naive Bayes, Linear SVM and Logistic Regression tie on F1 (0.591) because the test set has so few distinct sentences; Logistic Regression was chosen because it gives probabilities for the confidence score and its SHAP values can be computed exactly.

title: Data leakage and train/test split
text: The dataset has only 96 unique ticket messages repeated across all tickets, and each message always has the same category. A random train/test split therefore puts the same sentences in both sets and gives a misleading macro F1 of 1.0. The project splits by message instead (grouped split), so the test only contains unseen wording. The columns agent_first_reply and resolution_summary reveal the category and are never used as model inputs, and outcome columns such as status, sentiment and CSAT are only known after a ticket is handled.

title: How SHAP explanations work for the TF-IDF model
text: SHAP gives each word in a ticket a score for how much it pushed the prediction towards or away from a category. For the linear TF-IDF + Logistic Regression model the SHAP value of a word is its model weight times the difference between its TF-IDF value in the ticket and its average TF-IDF value. The values add up exactly to the model score. Some filler words such as 'my' and 'the' carry weight because the synthetic sentences are built from templates.

title: How SHAP works for the BGE embedding model (word-level, exact) and is it faithful
text: The BGE model sees a 768-number vector, so SHAP is computed at the word level: each word is a player, leaving a word out means deleting it from the sentence and embedding the shorter sentence again, and the value explained is the model's score (logit) per category. Messages have 8 to 14 words, so every subset of words is tried and the Shapley values are exact (221312 shortened sentences embedded for 96 messages). Checks: base value plus word values equals the model score within 3.6e-08, and the shap library's Exact explainer agrees within 1.1e-08. Deletion test: removing the top SHAP word lowers the predicted-class probability by 0.125 on average versus 0.026 for a random word; removing the top 3 lowers it by 0.519 versus 0.118 and changes the prediction for 40.6% of messages. Share of the explanation going to stop words: 27.4% for TF-IDF and 26.0% for BGE, while 51.9% of words are stop words. Most influential words overall with TF-IDF: how, plan, can, in the, on my, noticed suspicious, noticed, suspicious, login on, suspicious login, general, general question. With BGE: not, error, suspicious, vulnerability, i, password, my, encryption, export, data, crashing, how.

title: Notebook 1: Sampling, Data Cleaning and EDA: Introduction
text:
HCLTech Future Ready Data Science Hackathon, Use case 4: IT Support Ticket Classification and Analytics

The project goal is to predict the category of an IT support ticket from the message the customer writes,
and to build a dashboard that shows categories, trends, recurring issues and problem areas.

The full project runs in six notebooks:

| Notebook | What it does |
|---|---|
| **01 (this one)** | Take a 20,000-ticket sample, check quality, clean, explore |
| 02 | Train and compare classifiers (Logistic Regression, SVM, Naive Bayes) |
| 03 | Explain the model with SHAP |
| 04 | Find recurring issues with clustering |
| 05 | Detect anomalies |
| 06 | GenAI assistant (RAG) that answers questions about the results |

Before building any model, we want to understand the data properly: what is in it, what is wrong with it,
what is related to what, and what could mislead a model.

What this notebook covers:

1. Taking the sample, loading the data and understanding the columns
2. Data quality checks
3. Cleaning
4. Univariate analysis (one column at a time)
5. Class imbalance
6. Bivariate analysis (two columns at a time)
7. Correlation analysis
8. Data leakage
9. Summary

The raw file goes in `data/raw/`. Outputs are written to `data/processed/` and charts to `reports/figures/`.

title: Notebook 1: Sampling, Data Cleaning and EDA: 1. Load the data and take a sample
text:
The full file has 100,000 tickets. We work with a sample of **20,000** to keep everything fast and easy to rerun.

The sample is **stratified** by `issue_type`, which means each category keeps the same share it has in the full data.
A fixed random seed (42) means anyone running this gets exactly the same 20,000 tickets.

The category shares match the full data almost exactly, and all the different messages are still present in the sample.

### What each column means

Some columns are available the moment a ticket is created. Others only get filled in after an agent has worked on it.
This difference matters a lot later, because a model can only use what is known when a new ticket arrives.

| Column | Meaning | Group |
|---|---|---|
| ticket_id, customer_id | Identifiers | ID |
| initial_message | What the customer wrote | Input text |
| issue_type | Ticket category | Target |
| created_at, priority, channel, product_area, platform, region, customer_segment, sla_plan, has_attachment | Ticket details | Known at arrival |
| status, agent_first_reply, resolution_summary, resolution_time_hours, reopened, customer_sentiment, csat_score | What happened afterwards | Known only later |

title: Notebook 1: Sampling, Data Cleaning and EDA: 2. Data quality checks
text:
### 2.1 Missing values

Three columns have gaps. Before filling anything, let's see why they are empty.

The resolution columns are empty only for tickets that are open, in progress or on hold. Those tickets simply
haven't been resolved yet, so the gaps are expected and we leave them empty. Filling them would mean inventing data.

Region is missing for about 20% of tickets, and the share is the same in every channel, so it looks random.
We'll label these as "Unknown" so they still show up in filters.

### 2.2 Duplicates

There are no duplicate tickets. The messages, though, repeat a lot: 20,000 tickets use only 96 different sentences.
The tickets themselves are still different (different customers, dates and priorities), so we keep all rows.
We'll come back to this in the data leakage section, because it changes how we have to split the data.

### 2.3 Values and ranges

CSAT is a satisfaction score from 1 to 5, yet about 30% of tickets have a 0. Is that a very unhappy customer,
or a customer who never answered the survey? Comparing it with sentiment should tell us.

Scores 1 to 5 line up neatly with sentiment (very negative customers give 1 or 2, very positive ones give 5).
A score of 0 shows up for every sentiment, including very positive. So 0 means "not rated", and we'll treat it as missing.
If we left it in, the average CSAT would look much worse than it really is.

### 2.4 Dates and text

### Quality check summary

| Check | What we found | What we do |
|---|---|---|
| Missing resolution fields | Only for unfinished tickets | Leave empty |
| Missing region (20%) | Random | Fill with "Unknown" |
| Duplicate rows or IDs | None | Nothing |
| Repeated messages | Only 96 unique texts | Keep rows, handle when splitting |
| csat_score = 0 | Means "not rated" | Set to missing |
| Bad numbers, bad dates, empty text | None | Nothing |
| customer_id | Personal identifier, not useful here | Drop |

title: Notebook 1: Sampling, Data Cleaning and EDA: 4. Univariate analysis
text:
Here we look at one column at a time to see what values it takes and how they are spread.

### 4.1 The target: issue_type

Eight categories, each with roughly 12.5% of the tickets. Section 5 looks at balance in more detail.

### 4.2 Categorical columns

- channel, product_area, platform, region and customer_segment are split almost exactly evenly. Real support data is rarely this tidy, which is a hint that the data is synthetic.
- Priority is uneven: low 40%, medium 35%, high 20%, urgent 5%.
- Half the tickets are resolved and about 40% are still open, in progress or on hold.
- 42% of customers are negative or very negative.

### 4.3 Numeric columns

Resolution time has a long right tail. Every ticket above the IQR limit (about 106 hours) is a "closed_no_action" ticket,
meaning it was closed after the customer stopped replying. These aren't errors, they just measure something different
from a real fix. We keep them, and when we talk about how long fixes take we'll look at resolved tickets only.

About 5% of tickets get reopened and a quarter come with an attachment.

### 4.4 Message text

Messages are short, between 8 and 14 words. The most common sentences are generic ones ("I cannot log in...",
"I was charged twice...") repeated around 4,000 times each. Sentences that name a product
("The billing page is very slow...") appear about 600 times each.

### 4.5 Dates

Volume is flat from 2022 to 2025, at around 420 tickets a month in our sample. There's no busy weekday, no busy hour and no season.
Real helpdesks are much busier on weekday mornings, so this again points to synthetic timestamps.

title: Notebook 1: Sampling, Data Cleaning and EDA: 5. Class imbalance
text:
If one category had far more tickets than the others, a model could get a high accuracy just by predicting that
category most of the time, while doing badly on the small ones. So we check how even the classes are.

The classes are balanced. The biggest is only 1.03 times the smallest, and always guessing the biggest class
would give just 12.7% accuracy. So we don't need oversampling, SMOTE or class weights.
We'll still report macro F1 (every class counts equally) along with weighted F1, as the brief asks.

There is a less obvious imbalance though: how many *different* sentences each class has.

account_access, billing_problem and other each have only 3 different sentences, while bug, feature_request and how_to have 21.
The ticket counts are even, but the variety of wording isn't. A model gets very few examples of how people describe
the 3-sentence classes, so these are the ones most likely to fail on new wording. We'll treat them as the "minority"
classes to watch during evaluation.

title: Notebook 1: Sampling, Data Cleaning and EDA: 6. Bivariate analysis
text:
Now we look at two columns together. The main question is which columns are related to the target.

The tools:
- **Crosstab**: a table of counts or percentages for two categorical columns
- **Chi-square test**: tells us whether two categorical columns are related at all (p below 0.05 means related)
- **Cramér's V**: tells us how strong that relationship is, from 0 (none) to 1 (perfect)
- **Kruskal-Wallis test**: tells us whether a numeric column differs between groups (p below 0.05 means it does)

### 6.1 Target vs every categorical column

Almost nothing is related to the category. Priority, channel, product area, platform, region, segment, SLA plan,
attachments and weekday all have a Cramér's V of 0.02 or less. Every category gets the same mix of each.
The one exception is customer sentiment (V about 0.19), but sentiment is only known after the ticket is handled.

So the message text is the only useful input for predicting the category.

### 6.2 Target vs customer experience

This is the clearest real pattern in the data. Customers raising actual problems are much unhappier:

- security_concern, performance, account_access and billing_problem: about 60% negative, average CSAT around 2.8
- bug and other: about 30% negative, CSAT around 3.4
- how_to and feature_request: about 20% negative, CSAT around 3.7

Reopen rates are about 5% everywhere, so the unhappiness isn't coming from tickets bouncing back.
This is a good insight for the dashboard: the problem categories are where customer satisfaction needs attention.

### 6.3 Target vs resolution time

Every category takes about the same time to resolve (median around 23 hours, Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.89). The category doesn't change how fast a ticket gets fixed.

### 6.4 Priority vs resolution time

Priority is what drives resolution time: urgent tickets take about 4 hours, low ones about 40.
Each priority also has a hard ceiling (8, 24, 48 and 72 hours) that no ticket ever goes past, a bit like an SLA limit.
That kind of perfect compliance is another sign of generated data.

### 6.5 Volume over time by category

All categories stay flat and close together. No category is growing or fading over the four years.

### 6.6 Message text vs target

Every message always comes with the same category, so the text completely decides the label.
That's good news for learning, but it also creates a leakage risk, which section 8 deals with.

title: Notebook 1: Sampling, Data Cleaning and EDA: 7. Correlation analysis
text:
Correlation tells us which columns move together. We check it for three kinds of pairs, because each needs a different measure:

| Pair | Measure | Range |
|---|---|---|
| Numeric vs numeric | Pearson (straight-line relationship) and Spearman (any steady up/down relationship) | -1 to 1 |
| Categorical vs categorical | Cramér's V | 0 to 1 |
| Numeric vs categorical | Correlation ratio (eta): how much of the numeric column's spread is explained by the groups | 0 to 1 |

As a rough guide: below 0.1 is no real relationship, 0.1 to 0.3 is weak, 0.3 to 0.5 is moderate, and above 0.5 is strong.

### 7.1 Numeric vs numeric

Only two pairs are related; everything else is close to zero.

- **csat_score and sentiment_score** are strongly positive (about 0.9). They measure the same thing, the customer's mood, so in any analysis we should use one of them, not both.
- **priority_rank and resolution_time_hours** are negative: Spearman -0.47, but Pearson only -0.20. Higher priority means faster resolution.
  The gap between the two is a good example of why we check both. Pearson looks for a straight-line relationship and gets pulled
  around by the very long closed_no_action times, while Spearman only looks at the ranking, so it isn't thrown off by those extreme values.

Things that are *not* related are worth noting too: word count, hour of day and attachments have nothing to do with any other column,
and being reopened doesn't affect CSAT.

### 7.2 Categorical vs categorical

Almost every value is 0.02 or less. The only notable link is between issue_type and customer_sentiment (around 0.19, weak),
which is the "problem tickets are unhappier" pattern from section 6.2.

This also tells us there is no hidden relationship among the metadata columns themselves
(for example, enterprise customers don't use a particular channel more), so none of them is redundant with another.

### 7.3 Numeric vs categorical

A few clear relationships stand out:

- **status and resolution_time_hours** (about 0.8, strong): closed_no_action tickets take far longer than resolved ones, which is what we saw with the outliers.
- **issue_type and word_count** (about 0.4, moderate): each category is written with its own set of sentences, so message length differs by category. This comes from the text itself, which is our input anyway. product_area has a weak link (about 0.13) for the same reason, since product names change sentence length.
- **issue_type and csat_score** (about 0.33, moderate): the "problem tickets are unhappier" pattern again.
- **priority and resolution_time_hours** (about 0.2, weak here): weak only because the long closed_no_action times add a lot of spread. Among resolved tickets alone the effect is much stronger (section 6.4).

Everything else is close to zero.

### 7.4 What the correlation analysis tells us

- The category depends on the **text** and on nothing else that is known when a ticket arrives.
- csat_score and customer_sentiment are basically the same information; keep one in any analysis.
- Resolution time is explained by priority and status, not by category.
- There's no multicollinearity to worry about among the arrival columns, because they are all independent of each other.

title: Notebook 1: Sampling, Data Cleaning and EDA: 8. Data leakage
text:
Data leakage is when a model gets information during training that it wouldn't have when predicting a real new ticket.
The test scores then look great, but the model falls apart in real use. We check three ways this could happen here.

### 8.1 Columns that give away the answer

`agent_first_reply` and `resolution_summary` are written by the agent *after* they've read and categorised the ticket.

Each kind of reply belongs to exactly one category ("Thanks for reporting this bug" is only ever used for bugs),
and the same is true for the resolution summaries, apart from the generic "closed without action" one.
A model that could see these columns would simply read the answer off them, so they can't be used as inputs.

### 8.2 Information from the future

`status`, `resolution_time_hours`, `reopened`, `customer_sentiment` and `csat_score` only exist after the ticket has been handled.
Even though sentiment is somewhat related to category, we can't use it: when a new ticket comes in, nobody knows yet how the customer will feel.

### 8.3 The same message in training and testing

There are only 96 different messages. If we split tickets randomly into train and test, the same sentences end up on both sides.
The test would then only check whether the model *remembers* sentences it has already seen, not whether it can handle new ones.
Let's compare a random split with a split by message.

With a random split, every single test message was already in the training data, so any model would look close to perfect.
That score would be misleading. Splitting by message brings the overlap down to zero, and the test then measures
what we actually care about: how the model handles wording it hasn't seen.

So for modelling we'll **split by message**. One side effect: the test set ends up with uneven class sizes
(see the test counts per category above), and the 3-sentence classes are tested on a single sentence.
That's why we should look at per-class precision, recall and F1, not just overall accuracy.

### 8.4 Leakage summary

title: Notebook 1: Sampling, Data Cleaning and EDA: 9. Summary
text:
| Area | What we found | What we'll do |
|---|---|---|
| Quality | No duplicates, empty texts or impossible values | Light cleaning only |
| Missing values | Resolution fields empty only for unfinished tickets; region missing at random | Leave resolution empty; region as "Unknown" |
| Invalid values | csat_score = 0 means "not rated" | Treat as missing |
| Univariate | Even spreads, short messages, flat volume over time | Data is synthetic; say so in the report |
| Outliers | Long resolution times are all closed_no_action tickets | Keep them; use resolved tickets for fix times |
| Class balance | Balanced (ratio 1.03), but 3 classes have only 3 sentences each | No resampling; watch those 3 classes; use macro F1 |
| Bivariate | Arrival details are unrelated to category; the text decides it | Use the text only |
| Bivariate | Problem categories ~60% negative vs ~20% for requests; fix time depends on priority | Main insights for the dashboard |
| Correlation | csat and sentiment carry the same information; priority drives resolution time; arrival columns are independent | Keep one of csat/sentiment; no multicollinearity issue |
| Leakage | Agent reply and resolution summary give away the label; outcome columns are from the future | Exclude from model inputs |
| Leakage | Random split puts every test message in training | Split by message |

Saved: `data/processed/tickets_clean.csv` (used by every later notebook and the dashboard) and all charts in `reports/figures/`.

Next, notebook 02: split by message, start with a simple baseline, then compare Logistic Regression, SVM and Naive Bayes on TF-IDF features,
using per-class precision, recall and F1, macro and weighted F1, ROC-AUC and a confusion matrix.

title: Notebook 2: Ticket Classification (Supervised Machine Learning): Introduction
text:
**Task:** read a ticket message and predict its `issue_type`. There are 8 categories, so this is **multi-class classification**.

**Plan**
1. Turn the text into numbers with **TF-IDF**
2. Split the data **by message**, so the test set only has wording the model has never seen (we found in notebook 01 that a random split leaks)
3. Train and compare four models: a majority-class baseline, **Naive Bayes**, **Linear SVM** and **Logistic Regression**
4. Check the results are stable with grouped cross-validation
5. Look closely at the chosen model: precision, recall, F1, confusion matrix, ROC-AUC, confidence and mistakes
6. Save predictions and the final model for the dashboard

**How we measure success**

| Metric | What it tells us |
|---|---|
| Precision | When the model says "billing_problem", how often is it right? |
| Recall | Of all real billing tickets, how many did the model catch? |
| F1 | One number that balances precision and recall |
| Macro F1 | Average F1 over the 8 classes, every class counts equally (our main metric) |
| Weighted F1 | Average F1 weighted by class size |
| ROC-AUC | How well the model *ranks* the right class above the others, from 0.5 (guessing) to 1 (perfect) |

title: Notebook 2: Ticket Classification (Supervised Machine Learning): 1. Text to numbers: TF-IDF
text:
A model can't read words, so we convert each message into a vector of numbers.
**TF-IDF** gives every word (and pair of words) a score: high if it appears in this message but is rare across all messages,
low if it's common everywhere (like "the" or "my"). We use single words and word pairs (`ngram_range=(1, 2)`),
so phrases like "charged twice" or "timing out" are kept together.

title: Notebook 2: Ticket Classification (Supervised Machine Learning): 2. Train / test split by message
text:
Every message always has the same label, and the same 96 messages are repeated thousands of times.
So we split the **messages** (20% to test), and every ticket follows its message. The test set then only contains wording the model has never seen.
We stratify by category, so every category has messages on both sides.

### Why not a random split? A quick demonstration

Same model, two ways of splitting:

The random split gives a near-perfect score because the model has already seen every test sentence. That number says nothing
about new tickets. The split by message gives the honest number. Everything below uses the split by message.

title: Notebook 2: Ticket Classification (Supervised Machine Learning): 3. Train and compare the models
text:
| Model | Idea in one line |
|---|---|
| Majority baseline | Always predicts the most common class. Any real model must beat this. |
| Naive Bayes | Counts how often each word appears in each category and multiplies the chances. Fast and simple. |
| Linear SVM | Finds the boundary that separates the categories with the widest margin. |
| Logistic Regression | Learns a weight for every word per category and turns the total into probabilities. |

All four use the same TF-IDF features. The SVM doesn't output probabilities, so for ROC-AUC we convert its scores with a softmax.

All three real models beat the baseline by a wide margin (macro F1 0.61 vs 0.01), and they make **exactly the same predictions** on the test set.
That sounds strange but makes sense here: the test set is just 20 different sentences, and each model ends up putting each sentence in the same category.
They only differ in ROC-AUC, which looks at the full ranking of probabilities rather than just the top pick. Naive Bayes ranks slightly better (0.92 vs 0.89).

With so few distinct sentences, the choice of algorithm matters much less than the variety of wording the model has seen.

title: Notebook 2: Ticket Classification (Supervised Machine Learning): 4. Are the results stable? Grouped cross-validation
text:
The test set has only 20 messages, so one unlucky split could change the ranking. With **grouped 5-fold cross-validation**
every message is in the test fold exactly once, and a message never appears in train and test of the same fold.

Cross-validation tells the same story: all three models score a macro F1 of 0.59 (± 0.05 across folds), far above the baseline.
Since they're tied on F1, we pick **Logistic Regression** as the final model, because:

- it gives proper probabilities, which we need for the confidence score and the manual-review rule,
- each word gets a readable weight per category, so it's easy to explain,
- SHAP values for a linear model can be calculated exactly (notebook 03).

title: Notebook 2: Ticket Classification (Supervised Machine Learning): 5. A closer look at Logistic Regression
text:
### 5.1 Precision, recall and F1 per class

The results split into two groups:

- **Perfect on unseen wording:** billing_problem, bug, feature_request and performance. Their test sentences share key words with training sentences ("error", "add an option", "slow", "billed").
- **Complete misses:** account_access and other score 0. Each has only 3 sentences in total, so the model learned 2 and was tested on a third that uses different words.
- how_to and security_concern have perfect recall but low precision, because they absorb the tickets from the two missed classes.

This is the "hidden imbalance" from notebook 01 showing up: classes with very little variety in wording don't generalise.

### 5.2 Confusion matrix

Both big mistakes are understandable when you read the sentences:

- "My account was locked after multiple failed login attempts" goes to **security_concern**, because the training data only had "login" in the security sentence "I noticed a suspicious **login** on my account".
- "I need help but I'm not sure which category this fits in" goes to **how_to**, because "I need help setting up..." is a how_to sentence.

The model is matching words, not meaning. More varied training wording, or sentence embeddings that capture meaning, would help these two classes most.

### 5.3 ROC curves and ROC-AUC per class

Macro ROC-AUC is 0.89, much better than random (0.5). So even when the top pick is wrong, the right category is usually ranked high.
The two classes with zero F1 have the lowest AUC, which is consistent with the confusion matrix.

### 5.4 Confidence: can the model tell when it's unsure?

The confidence of a prediction is the probability of the top class. If the model is sensible, low-confidence predictions
should be wrong more often. Then we can send them to a person instead of forcing a category (requirement FR-04).

Confidence helps, but it's not perfect. Tickets above the 60% threshold are right 71% of the time, while those below it are right only 49% of the time,
so the review rule does catch a large share of mistakes.

But one fully correct group (billing tickets with new wording) sits at low confidence, and one wrong group (other → how_to) sits at 60–70%.
With only 20 test sentences, each sentence moves a whole bar. In practice, the threshold should be tuned on more varied real tickets.

### 5.5 Worked examples

The brief asks for examples covering a common ticket, an ambiguous one, a minority category and a low-confidence case.
Here we use the model trained on the training messages, so these sentences are new to it (except the first one).

- **Common:** a known sentence is classified with 99% confidence and routed straight to the Service Desk.
- **Ambiguous:** a message mixing "slow" and "error" goes to performance (71%), with bug as the runner-up. A person might reasonably pick either.
- **Minority class, new wording:** the account-lockout ticket gets only 47% confidence, so it goes to manual review instead of the wrong team. That's the review rule doing its job.
- **Out of scope:** a coffee machine complaint gets 46% confidence and is sent to review rather than forced into a category.

`model_comparison.csv`, `cv_scores.csv`, `metrics.json`, and the final model `models/tfidf_logreg.joblib`.

**Limitation to mention:** the scores reflect how the model handles *new wording*. With only 96 sentences, that's a tough test.
Real ticket data with more varied wording would very likely score higher.

title: Notebook 2b: Semantic Embeddings for Ticket Classification: Introduction
text:
Notebook 02 found that TF-IDF models **match words, not meaning**. For example, "My account was locked after multiple failed
**login** attempts" went to security_concern only because the word "login" appeared in a security sentence.

Here we replace TF-IDF with **sentence embeddings**: pre-trained neural models that turn a sentence into a vector so that
sentences with similar *meaning* get similar vectors, even when they share no words.

**Plan**
1. Use the same data, the same split by message and the same grouped 5-fold CV as notebook 02, so the scores can be compared directly
2. Build four text representations: TF-IDF (the notebook 02 baseline) and three sentence-embedding models
3. Train the same set of classifiers on each one: Logistic Regression, Linear SVM, k-Nearest Neighbours, Random Forest (+ Naive Bayes for TF-IDF)
4. Compare every combination on accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and ROC-AUC
5. Look closely at the best combination: per-class scores, confusion matrix, the hard sentences from notebook 02 and the confidence rule

**Requirements:** `pip install sentence-transformers`. The first run downloads the three models (about 0.6 GB in total) from Hugging Face.

title: Notebook 2b: Semantic Embeddings for Ticket Classification: 2. Four ways to turn text into numbers
text:
| Representation | Type | Size | Idea |
|---|---|---|---|
| **TF-IDF** (notebook 02) | word counts | ~400 | One number per word / word pair. Two sentences are similar only if they share words. |
| **all-MiniLM-L6-v2** | sentence embedding | 384 | Small, fast transformer trained on 1 billion sentence pairs to put paraphrases close together. |
| **all-mpnet-base-v2** | sentence embedding | 768 | Larger model from the same family; usually better quality than MiniLM. |
| **BAAI/bge-base-en-v1.5** | sentence embedding | 768 | Newer model trained for retrieval and similarity; among the strongest models of its size. |

The embedding models are used as they are (no fine-tuning). Each vector is scaled to length 1, so the dot product of two vectors is their cosine similarity.
Only the 96 unique messages need to be encoded; every ticket then reuses its message's vector.

### Do the embeddings capture meaning? A quick check

Below are the two sentences notebook 02 got wrong. For each one we list its closest **training** sentences, once with TF-IDF and once with BGE.

TF-IDF finds training sentences that **share words** ("login", "account", "I need help"), even when they mean something different. BGE finds sentences with the **same meaning**:

- The lockout sentence's closest neighbour is "I cannot log in; the system says my password is incorrect" (account_access, similarity 0.79). TF-IDF's closest is the *suspicious login* sentence (security_concern).
- The "not sure which category" sentence lands next to two other `other` sentences ("I have a general question…", "Something seems off…"). TF-IDF puts it next to three how_to sentences that start with "I need help".

This is the notebook 02 failure, fixed at the level of the representation.

title: Notebook 2b: Semantic Embeddings for Ticket Classification: 3. Training setup
text:
Every ticket that uses the same message has the same text and the same label. So instead of training on 15,000+ duplicate rows, we train on the
**unique training messages, weighted by how many tickets use them**. For Logistic Regression, SVM, Naive Bayes and Random Forest this gives the
same model as training on every ticket, and it is about 100 times faster. (Check: the TF-IDF models below reproduce notebook 02's CV score exactly.)
k-Nearest Neighbours is the exception: it simply looks up the 3 most similar training *messages*.

All scores are still computed **per ticket**, exactly as in notebook 02.

| Classifier | Idea in one line |
|---|---|
| Logistic Regression | One weight per feature per category, turned into probabilities |
| Linear SVM | Widest-margin linear boundary (scores turned into probabilities with a softmax for ROC-AUC) |
| k-Nearest Neighbours | Vote of the 3 most similar training messages (cosine similarity, closer counts more) |
| Random Forest | 300 decision trees voting; can learn non-linear rules |
| Naive Bayes | Word-count model; only used with TF-IDF, because it needs non-negative features |

title: Notebook 2b: Semantic Embeddings for Ticket Classification: 4. Results on the holdout test set (20 unseen messages)
text:
On the 20 holdout messages, **BGE with Logistic Regression, SVM or Random Forest gets every ticket right** (macro F1 1.00). MiniLM and MPNet reach 0.82, and every TF-IDF model stays at 0.61 or lower. The TF-IDF + LR score matches notebook 02 exactly (0.611), which confirms the setup is the same.

But 20 messages is a tiny test, and one sentence moves macro F1 by 0.1 or more. The grouped cross-validation below is the result to trust.

title: Notebook 2b: Semantic Embeddings for Ticket Classification: 5. Grouped 5-fold cross-validation (the main result)
text:
The holdout test has only 20 messages, so one sentence can move macro F1 a lot. Grouped CV tests every one of the 96 messages exactly once,
always with a model that never saw it. We report:
- the **mean and spread of macro F1 across the 5 folds** (same as `cv_scores.csv` from notebook 02), and
- scores on the **out-of-fold predictions for all 20,000 tickets** (same as `metrics.json` from notebook 02).

**Main findings**

- **Sentence embeddings clearly beat TF-IDF.** The best combinations are BGE + Linear SVM (macro F1 **0.82**) and BGE + Logistic Regression (**0.81**). Every TF-IDF model is stuck at **0.59**. That is a gain of about +0.22.
- **A better embedding model helps a lot.** With Logistic Regression: MiniLM 0.71, then MPNet 0.79, then BGE 0.81.
- **Linear classifiers work best on embeddings.** Random Forest is the weakest on average (0.55–0.69). In an embedding, meaning is spread over hundreds of dimensions, and trees that split on one dimension at a time can't use it well with only ~77 training sentences.
- **kNN depends heavily on embedding quality:** 0.80 with BGE but only 0.55–0.59 with MiniLM / MPNet. With BGE, similarity on its own is almost enough to find the right category.
- **Ranking quality jumps:** out-of-fold ROC-AUC goes from 0.86 (TF-IDF + LR) to 0.99 (BGE + LR). The right category is almost always at or near the top.
- **Fold-to-fold spread is larger** (±0.09–0.10 vs ±0.05). Each fold has only ~19 messages, and with BGE the remaining errors are a handful of hard sentences that land in some folds and not others.

*Caveat:* we picked the best of 17 combinations on the same CV, so 0.81–0.82 is slightly optimistic. The gap to TF-IDF is much bigger than that effect.

title: Notebook 2b: Semantic Embeddings for Ticket Classification: 6. A closer look: BGE + Logistic Regression vs TF-IDF + Logistic Regression
text:
We pick **BGE + Logistic Regression** for the deep dive: it is tied for the best CV score with BGE + SVM, and like in notebook 02
Logistic Regression gives proper probabilities for the confidence rule. All numbers below use out-of-fold predictions
(every ticket predicted by a model that never saw its message).

### 6.1 Per-class F1

- The two classes TF-IDF **completely missed** improve the most: **account_access 0.00 to 0.80** and **other 0.00 to 0.49**.
- billing_problem goes from 0.41 to 0.86, how_to from 0.67 to 1.00, security_concern from 0.40 to 0.66.
- No single model wins every class. MPNet is better on security_concern (0.80) and billing_problem (1.00), and BGE is better on how_to and other.
- feature_request drops from 1.00 to 0.86. Its recall is still 100%, but one security sentence about "data encryption and compliance" is now predicted as a feature request (see 6.3).
- `other` remains the hardest class. Its sentences are vague by design ("Something seems off…"), so their meaning really does overlap with other categories.

### 6.2 Confusion matrix (BGE + LR, out-of-fold)

### 6.3 Which sentences changed?

Every unique message with its out-of-fold prediction under both models, showing only the ones where at least one model is wrong.

- BGE **fixes 6 of the 10 messages** TF-IDF got wrong and **breaks none**.
- Fixed: both notebook 02 examples ("account was locked…" now goes to account_access, "not sure which category…" now goes to other), plus "I was charged twice…", which TF-IDF had sent to how_to.
- Still wrong (4 messages):
  - "My 2FA code is not working when I try to sign in" goes to bug (73% confidence). That is an understandable mistake, since "not working" sounds like a bug.
  - Two vague `other` sentences, at very low confidence (26% and 31%), so they would go to manual review.
  - "We need details about your data encryption and compliance" goes to feature_request (58%), also below the review threshold.
- So **3 of the 4 remaining mistakes would be caught by the manual-review rule**.
- Why is ticket-level F1 (0.82) lower than 92/96 messages would suggest? The hard messages are in the small classes, where each message stands for ~830 tickets, so every wrong message costs a lot of tickets.

### 6.4 Does the confidence rule still work?

Same rule as notebook 02: below 60% confidence the ticket goes to manual review.

- **The share of tickets sent to manual review drops from 46% to 17%**, cutting the manual triage workload by almost two thirds.
- Auto-routed tickets are right **95%** of the time (vs 92% with TF-IDF).
- Overall accuracy goes from **58% to 83%**.
- Reviewed tickets are mostly wrong (25% accuracy), which is what we want: the rule is catching the mistakes.

title: Notebook 2b: Semantic Embeddings for Ticket Classification: Summary
text:
| Item | TF-IDF + LR (notebook 02) | BGE + LR (this notebook) |
|---|---|---|
| Features | word / word-pair counts (~400) | pre-trained sentence embedding (768) |
| Grouped CV macro F1 (mean ± std) | 0.59 ± 0.05 | **0.81 ± 0.10** |
| Out-of-fold macro F1 / accuracy | 0.54 / 0.58 | **0.82 / 0.83** |
| Out-of-fold macro ROC-AUC | 0.86 | **0.99** |
| account_access / other F1 | 0.00 / 0.00 | **0.80 / 0.49** |
| Sent to manual review | 46% | **17%** |
| Auto-routed accuracy | 92% | **95%** |

**Ranking of representations (best classifier each, grouped CV):** BGE 0.82 > MPNet 0.79 > MiniLM 0.71 > TF-IDF 0.59.
**Ranking of classifiers on embeddings:** Linear SVM ≈ Logistic Regression > kNN > Random Forest.

**Trade-offs**
- Embeddings need `sentence-transformers` (PyTorch) and a ~440 MB model. TF-IDF + LR is tiny and instant.
- SHAP values on embedding dimensions don't map to words. Word-level SHAP for this model is computed in notebook 03b (each word deleted and the sentence re-embedded), which is slower than the instant TF-IDF formula.
- With only 96 sentences, all these scores come from very little data. Real tickets with more varied wording are needed to confirm the ranking.

**Saved:** `data/processed/embedding_holdout_comparison.csv`, `embedding_cv_scores.csv`, `embedding_per_class_f1.csv`, `embedding_class_report.csv`, `embedding_confidence_rule.csv`, `embedding_message_changes.csv`, `embedding_metrics.json`, figures `25`–`27`, and `models/bge_logreg.joblib` (BGE + LR trained on all messages). The dashboard still uses the TF-IDF model from notebook 02.

title: Notebook 3: Explaining the Model with SHAP: Introduction
text:
A prediction is more useful when we can say *why* the model made it. **SHAP** (SHapley Additive exPlanations) gives every word
in a message a score for how much it pushed the prediction towards (positive) or away from (negative) a category.

A few things that make SHAP easy to trust here:

- For a **linear model** like our Logistic Regression, SHAP values can be calculated exactly with a simple formula:
  `SHAP(word) = model weight of the word × (word's TF-IDF value in this message − its average TF-IDF value)`.
  This is exactly what `shap.LinearExplainer` computes, so we write it out ourselves. It's transparent and needs no extra library.
- SHAP values **add up**: the average model score plus all the word contributions equals the model's score for that message. We check this below.

We look at two levels:
- **Global**: which words matter most for each category overall
- **Local**: why one particular ticket got its prediction

title: Notebook 3: Explaining the Model with SHAP: 1. Calculate the SHAP values
text:
The "average message" (the background) is the mean TF-IDF vector over all 20,000 tickets.
Because the same 96 sentences repeat, we calculate SHAP once per unique sentence and remember how many tickets each one stands for.

The difference is essentially zero, so the explanations add up exactly to what the model computes.

**Optional cross-check with the `shap` library.** If you have it installed (`pip install shap`), this cell compares our numbers
with `shap.LinearExplainer`. If it isn't installed, the cell just says so.

title: Notebook 3: Explaining the Model with SHAP: 2. Global view: which words drive each category?
text:
For each category we average the SHAP values of the tickets that belong to it (weighted by how many tickets use each sentence).
Words with a high average push tickets into that category.

Most of the top words are what a human agent would look for:

- **account_access**: "locked", "failed login", "login attempts"
- **billing_problem**: "plan", "charged twice", "subscription"
- **bug**: "saving", "not saving", "error" ("seeing an error")
- **feature_request**: "option", "customize", "add an"
- **security_concern**: "suspicious", "noticed suspicious", "vulnerability"
- **performance**: "timing out", "queries", "module"

But there's also a warning sign. Some filler words rank high too: "after" for account_access, "in the" and "are" for performance, "my changes" for bug.
They appear in only one category's sentences, so the model treats them as clues. That's a side effect of the dataset being built from a small set of sentences,
and it's one reason the model struggles with new wording. Product names (billing, notifications, ...) are *not* near the top, which is good.

The overall ranking confirms the warning. The most influential words across all categories are common words like "my", "the", "in the", "can" and "for".
On their own they say nothing about the problem; they matter here only because each sentence template uses them differently.
With real, varied tickets this effect would shrink. A next step would be to test stop-word removal or sentence embeddings with more diverse training text.
(We tried removing stop words in testing; on this dataset it lowered macro F1, so we kept them.)

title: Notebook 3: Explaining the Model with SHAP: 3. Local view: why did this ticket get this prediction?
text:
We explain a few messages. For each one we show the words that pushed hardest towards the predicted category (positive)
and against it (negative). The new sentences were written by us and are not in the dataset.

- **"charged twice"** (billing_problem, 99%): "charged twice", "subscription" and "this month" all push towards billing.
- **The lockout sentence** (account_access, 66%) is new wording, but "locked" and "password" carry it to the right category.
- **"export page crashes and the invoice is wrong"** (performance, 37%) mixes two problems. "page" pulls it towards the "page is very slow" sentences, while "invoice" pulls against.
  The low confidence correctly tells us a person should look at it.
- **"How do I reset my password?"** (account_access, 40%): "password" pushes towards access, while "how" pushes towards how_to. It's a genuinely ambiguous ticket,
  and the explanation shows exactly which words pull it each way.

This is what the dashboard shows next to each live prediction.

title: Notebook 3: Explaining the Model with SHAP: Summary
text:
- SHAP values were calculated exactly for the Logistic Regression model, and we confirmed they add up to the model's scores.
- **Globally**, each category is driven mostly by sensible key words (locked/login attempts for access, charged twice/subscription for billing, timing out for performance).
- Some filler words ("my", "the", "after") also carry weight because of how the synthetic sentences were written. This is a known limitation to mention.
- **Locally**, explanations show which words pushed a ticket each way, which makes mixed or vague tickets easy to understand.
- The background vector is saved, so the dashboard can explain brand-new tickets the same way.

Saved: `shap_global.csv`, `shap_local.csv`, `models/shap_background.npy`.

title: Notebook 3b: Explaining the Embedding Model with SHAP: Introduction
text:
Notebook 02b showed that **BGE sentence embeddings + Logistic Regression** classify much better than TF-IDF (macro F1 0.81 vs 0.59).
This notebook explains *why* it predicts what it predicts, using SHAP, the same way notebook 03 did for the TF-IDF model.

**The challenge.** The BGE model sees a 768-number vector, not words. SHAP values for "dimension 412" would mean nothing to a support agent.
So we explain the **whole pipeline** (text → BGE → Logistic Regression) in terms of the **words** of the message:

- A "player" in the Shapley game is one word of the message.
- Leaving a word out means **deleting it from the sentence** and embedding the shorter sentence again.
- The value being explained is the model's **score (logit) for each category**, the same quantity notebook 03 explains.
- The starting point (base value) is the score of an empty message.

Messages are short (8 to 14 words), so we can try **every** subset of words and get **exact** Shapley values, not an approximation.
Like in notebook 03, the values add up exactly: base value + sum of word contributions = the model's score. We check this below.

**Requirements:** `sentence-transformers` (same as notebook 02b) and `models/bge_logreg.joblib` from notebook 02b. The `shap` library is optional (cross-check only).
**Runtime:** about 5 minutes on an Apple-silicon GPU, about 12 minutes on CPU (around 270,000 short sentences to embed).

title: Notebook 3b: Explaining the Embedding Model with SHAP: 1. Calculate exact word-level SHAP values
text:
For a message with *n* words we score all 2<sup>n</sup> versions of it (every combination of words kept or deleted) and apply the Shapley formula:

`SHAP(word) = Σ over subsets S without the word: weight(|S|) × [ score(S + word) − score(S) ]`, with `weight(s) = s! (n − s − 1)! / n!`

Every shortened sentence is embedded once and remembered, because many of them repeat across messages (for example the 7 product versions of a sentence share most subsets).

**Optional cross-check with the `shap` library.** `shap.explainers.Exact` computes exact Shapley values for any function. We give it the same
"keep / delete each word" switches and compare on a few messages. If `shap` isn't installed the cell just says so.

title: Notebook 3b: Explaining the Embedding Model with SHAP: 2. Global view: which words drive each category?
text:
Same method as notebook 03: for each category we average the SHAP values (towards that category) over the category's tickets, weighted by how many tickets use each sentence.
Words are lower-cased and stripped of punctuation, so "attempts." and "attempts" count as one word.

In every category, the **top 3 words are words a human agent would look for**:

- **account_access:** password, 2fa, locked (then cannot, failed, sign in)
- **billing_problem:** charged, plan, billed, downgraded, twice
- **bug:** error, crashing, saving, not (as in "not saving")
- **feature_request:** customize, options, option
- **how_to:** how, setting, export, configure
- **other:** question, workspace, general
- **performance:** slow, timing, degraded, queries
- **security_concern:** suspicious, vulnerability, encryption

In notebook 03, filler words such as "after", "in the" and "are" made the TF-IDF top lists. Filler words still appear lower down here ("my" for other, "we" for security_concern), but none reaches a top 3.

### Do filler words still matter? Comparison with the TF-IDF model

Notebook 03 found that the TF-IDF model leans on filler words ("my", "the", "in the", "after"). Here we compare both models on the same footing:
for every message we take the SHAP values of the **words that are in the message**, towards the **predicted** category, and measure how much of the total
(absolute) contribution goes to **stop words** (common words such as "the", "my", "after", "in" from scikit-learn's English list).
For TF-IDF a word pair counts as a stop word only if both words are stop words.

- **Overall, both models lean on stop words about equally:** 27% of the explanation for TF-IDF and 26% for BGE, while about half of all words in the messages are stop words. BGE does **not** simply ignore common words.
- The difference is **which words carry the most weight** (chart):
  - TF-IDF's top 20 is dominated by word pairs from the three one-off sentences ("suspicious login", "general question", "about my", "on my"), plus "how", "can" and "in the".
  - BGE's top 20 is mostly problem words: error, suspicious, vulnerability, password, encryption, crashing, saving, 2fa, locked, slow, charged.
- Some of BGE's stop words carry meaning in context:
  - "not" (as in "not saving", "not working") is its single most influential word.
  - "how" marks how-to questions.
  - "in" comes from "sign in".
- "I" and "my" are true filler. The synthetic templates differ in whether they are written in the first person, and the model picks that up. This is the same dataset limitation notebook 03 described.

title: Notebook 3b: Explaining the Embedding Model with SHAP: 3. Local view: why did this ticket get this prediction?
text:
The same four new sentences as notebook 03 (written by us, not in the dataset), plus the lockout sentence that TF-IDF got wrong.
For each one we show both models' predictions, then the BGE explanation towards its predicted category.

- **"Charged twice":** both models are sure (99%). BGE relies on "charged", "twice", "month" and "subscription".
- **New wording for the lockout:** confidence rises from 66% (TF-IDF) to **98%** (BGE). "Locked", "password", "wrong" and "entering" drive it. They mean the same as the training sentence even though the wording differs.
- **"The export page crashes and the invoice is wrong":**
  - TF-IDF guessed performance (37%). BGE says **bug (69%)** because of "crashes" and "page", while "invoice" pulls the other way.
  - The ticket really mixes two problems. At 69% it would be auto-routed to the bug team even though half of it is a billing issue. That is a limit of giving each ticket a single label, and the explanation makes it visible.
- **"How do I reset my password?":** TF-IDF was unsure (40%, so manual review). BGE is confident (**92%** account_access), driven by "password" and "reset". That's a reasonable call, though some teams would file it as how_to.

title: Notebook 3b: Explaining the Embedding Model with SHAP: 4. Are the explanations faithful? A deletion test
text:
If SHAP really finds the words the model relies on, deleting the top SHAP words should hurt the prediction much more than deleting random words.
For each of the 96 messages we delete the 1, 2 or 3 words with the highest SHAP value towards the predicted category, and compare with deleting
the same number of random words (average of 20 random draws). We measure how much the probability of the original prediction drops.

- Deleting the single top-SHAP word lowers the confidence of the original prediction by **12 points** on average, vs **3 points** for a random word, about 5 times more.
- Deleting the top 3 SHAP words lowers it by **52 points** (vs 12 for random words) and changes the prediction for **41%** of messages.
- So the explanations point to words the model really depends on. They aren't just plausible-looking.

title: Notebook 3b: Explaining the Embedding Model with SHAP: Summary
text:
| | Notebook 03 (TF-IDF + LR) | Notebook 3b (BGE + LR) |
|---|---|---|
| Method | exact linear SHAP on TF-IDF features | exact Shapley values over words (each word deleted and the sentence re-embedded) |
| Additivity check (largest error) | 2e-14 | 4e-8 (float precision of the embedding model) |
| Matches the `shap` library | not checked (not installed) | yes, within 1e-8 |
| Top words per category | mostly key words, some filler in the top lists ("after", "in the") | key words in every top 3 |
| Stop-word share of the explanation | 27% | 26% |
| Deletion test | – | the top word matters about 5 times more than a random word |
| Cost | instant | ~4 minutes for all 96 messages on an Apple GPU; a few seconds for one new ticket |

**Limitations**
- Each word gets its own value. When words only work together ("not" + "saving", "sign" + "in"), the Shapley rule splits the credit between them.
- Trying every subset of words only works for short messages (2<sup>n</sup> versions). For long real tickets, use a sampling explainer such as `shap`'s Permutation or Partition explainer.
- Removing a word can produce ungrammatical text. That is standard for text SHAP, but it means the model is sometimes scored on sentences it would never see.

**Saved:** `data/processed/shap_bge_global.csv` and `shap_bge_local.csv` (same layout as notebook 03's files), plus `shap_bge_examples.csv`, `shap_bge_deletion_test.csv`, `shap_overall_comparison.csv` and `shap_bge_checks.json`, figures `33`–`35`. The dashboard still shows the TF-IDF explanations from notebook 03.

title: Notebook 4: Recurring Issue Detection (Unsupervised Clustering): Introduction
text:
The classifier tells us the category. Inside a category there are usually a few **recurring problems**: for example, inside "bug"
some people say a page crashes, others that changes don't save. Finding these themes tells the support team what keeps coming back.

There are no labels for themes, so this is **unsupervised learning**: we group tickets whose descriptions are similar.

**Method**
1. Turn each description into a **text embedding**, a short list of numbers where similar sentences get similar vectors.
   We use TF-IDF followed by TruncatedSVD (also called LSA, latent semantic analysis), which compresses the words into 30 "topic" dimensions.
2. Group the embeddings with **K-Means**.
3. Choose the number of groups with the **silhouette score** (how much closer each point is to its own group than to the next one; higher is better).
4. Describe each group with its top words and example tickets, and check that each group really is one coherent problem.

*Optional:* set `USE_SENTENCE_TRANSFORMERS = True` to use a pre-trained sentence-embedding model (`all-MiniLM-L6-v2`) instead of LSA.
It needs `pip install sentence-transformers` and an internet connection the first time. The results below use LSA.

title: Notebook 4: Recurring Issue Detection (Unsupervised Clustering): 2. First attempt: cluster all categories together
text:
Clustering everything at once works reasonably well (most clusters belong to one category), but it has two problems:

- a few clusters mix categories, because short sentences get grouped by shared surface words ("my account", "page") as much as by the actual problem;
- the silhouette score keeps rising as k grows, so there's no clear "natural" number of groups. Any k we pick would be somewhat arbitrary.

Since we already know each ticket's category, a cleaner approach is to **find themes within each category**. That answers the question
the support team actually asks: "what keeps coming up in bug tickets?"

title: Notebook 4: Recurring Issue Detection (Unsupervised Clustering): 3. Themes within each category
text:
For each category we try k = 2 up to 6 and keep the k with the best silhouette score.
If no k reaches a silhouette of 0.1, the sentences are too different to merge sensibly, so each sentence becomes its own theme.

Categories built from product-specific sentences (bug, feature_request, how_to, performance) split cleanly into 3 themes each, with high silhouette scores.
Categories with only a handful of very different sentences (account_access, billing_problem, other) don't group well (silhouette ≈ 0), so each sentence is its own theme.

title: Notebook 4: Recurring Issue Detection (Unsupervised Clustering): 4. Describe each theme
text:
**Is each theme coherent?** The cohesion column is the average cosine similarity between a theme's sentences and the theme centre.
A value near 1 means the sentences all say nearly the same thing. Reading the examples confirms each theme is one recognisable problem:

- **bug**: pages crashing, changes not saving, error messages on click
- **performance**: pages very slow to load, queries timing out, plus the general "performance has degraded" complaint
- **feature_request**: "add an option to customise", "more advanced options", "support for X"
- **how_to**: exporting data, setting things up for a team, configuring properly
- **security_concern**: vulnerabilities in a feature, suspicious logins, encryption and compliance questions

All themes are similar in size (roughly 760 to 880 tickets each), because the synthetic data spreads tickets evenly. In real data the sizes would differ a lot,
and the biggest themes would be the first candidates for a permanent fix or a self-service article.

title: Notebook 4: Recurring Issue Detection (Unsupervised Clustering): 5. Where do the themes sit? A 2-D map
text:
Squeezing 30 dimensions into 2 loses detail, but you can see small tight groups: the 7 product versions of each sentence sit together,
and sentences from the same category are mostly near each other. The single generic sentences sit on their own.

title: Notebook 4: Recurring Issue Detection (Unsupervised Clustering): 6. Are any themes growing?
text:
No theme is clearly growing or shrinking; they all move around the same level. That matches the flat volume we saw in notebook 01.
In real data, this chart is where a new problem (say, after a software release) would first show up.

title: Notebook 4: Recurring Issue Detection (Unsupervised Clustering): Summary
text:
- Descriptions were turned into **text embeddings** (TF-IDF + LSA) and grouped with **K-Means**, choosing k with the silhouette score.
- Clustering all categories together mixed categories, so we cluster **within each category**, which answers "what keeps coming up in this category".
- The result is a set of coherent recurring themes, each with top words, a ticket count, a cohesion score and example descriptions.
- Theme volumes are stable over time in this synthetic data; the trend chart is ready to catch a growing theme in real data.

Saved: `clusters.csv` (theme for every ticket) and `cluster_summary.csv` (one row per theme).

title: Notebook 4b: Recurring Issues with Semantic Embeddings: Introduction
text:
Notebook 04 found recurring themes by clustering **TF-IDF + LSA** vectors, which measure *shared words*.
Notebook 02b showed that **BGE sentence embeddings** capture *meaning* much better for classification. Here we redo the clustering with BGE and ask:

1. What makes two tickets "similar" in each representation?
2. Do the recurring themes within each category change?
3. Does meaning-based clustering show anything new?

**Method:** same as notebook 04 (K-Means, number of groups chosen with the silhouette score, tickets as weights), only the embedding changes.
We recompute the LSA vectors exactly as notebook 04 did, so the two can be compared side by side.

**Requirements:** `sentence-transformers` (same as notebook 02b).

title: Notebook 4b: Recurring Issues with Semantic Embeddings: 1. What makes two tickets similar?
text:
84 of the 96 sentences are built from **12 templates × 7 products**, e.g. "The *billing* page is very slow…" / "The *mobile app* page is very slow…".
So there are two ways two sentences can be alike: the **same problem** (template) about different products, or the **same product** with a different problem.
We compare the average cosine similarity of these pairs in both representations.

- Both representations rate **same problem, different product** highest. That's why the themes within each category (which follow the problem) come out mostly the same as in notebook 04 (section 4).
- The big difference is the middle column. BGE rates two sentences about the **same product** as fairly similar (0.71) even when the problem differs, while LSA barely does (0.26). BGE knows that "the billing page is slow" and "how do I configure billing" are both about billing.
- BGE similarities have a **high floor**: even unrelated sentences score 0.53, because they are all short English support messages. LSA gives them 0.00. So BGE clusters are less sharply separated, which shows up as lower silhouette scores below. BGE numbers should be compared with each other, not with LSA's.

title: Notebook 4b: Recurring Issues with Semantic Embeddings: 2. Clustering all categories together
text:
As in notebook 04 we cluster all 96 sentences at once for a range of k and record two numbers:
- **silhouette**: how clearly separated the groups are (higher is better),
- **purity**: the share of a cluster's tickets that come from its most common category, averaged over clusters (1 = every cluster is a single category).

- **Purity: BGE wins at coarse levels.** With 8 clusters, 79% of a BGE cluster's tickets come from one category, vs 66% for LSA. With 4 clusters it's 61% vs 42%. Groups built on meaning line up with the support categories much better.
- **Silhouette: LSA wins**, rising to 0.40 at k = 24. LSA puts the 7 product versions of each template almost on top of each other (they share nearly every word), so around k = 24 each template becomes its own perfect cluster. BGE's high similarity floor gives lower silhouettes everywhere (0.06–0.19).
- Neither silhouette curve points to a natural number of groups across all categories, the same conclusion as notebook 04. We keep the within-category themes (section 4) as the main result, and use the cross-category clustering below for a different question.

title: Notebook 4b: Recurring Issues with Semantic Embeddings: 3. A new view: product-area topics across categories
text:
Because BGE also groups sentences by **what they are about**, clustering across categories gives a different, useful view.
We ask for 8 clusters (the same number as categories) and look at what ends up together.

With 8 clusters, BGE groups tickets by **subject and intent**, not by category:

| Topic | What's in it | Tickets |
|---|---|---|
| **Something is broken** | bug, performance and vulnerability reports, plus "export my data" how-tos, mostly for products other than login | 4,886 |
| **Requests and set-up** | all feature requests plus "set up / configure" how-tos | 3,690 |
| **Login and sign-in** | all account_access tickets plus 8 of the 12 "login auth" sentences (crashes, slowness, set-up, vulnerability…) | 3,460 |
| **Billing and payments** | all billing_problem tickets plus 4 "billing" sentences (error, not saving, configure, vulnerability) | 2,992 |
| **Vague account questions** | the two general `other` sentences plus "I noticed a suspicious login on my account" | 2,473 |
| three single sentences | degraded performance, encryption and compliance, "check my workspace" | ~830 each |

**Why this is useful**
- **A subject-area view for teams.** The identity team would see 3,460 tickets about login, although only 2,522 are labelled account_access. The other 938 sit in bug, performance, how_to and security_concern. Billing is the same: 2,992 tickets vs 2,476 labelled billing_problem. Reporting by category alone hides this.
- **Only login and billing form areas of their own**, because those product names match the meaning of a whole category. The other five products stay spread over the "broken" and "requests" topics.
- It matches the classifier's remaining confusion in notebook 02b: `other` and security_concern sentences sit close together here.

title: Notebook 4b: Recurring Issues with Semantic Embeddings: 4. Recurring themes within each category
text:
Exactly the notebook 04 rule: for each category try k = 2 to 6, keep the k with the best silhouette, and if no k reaches 0.10, every sentence is its own theme.
We also measure how much the result agrees with notebook 04's themes (**adjusted Rand index**: 1 = identical grouping, 0 = no better than chance).

- **5 of 8 categories get exactly the same themes as notebook 04** (ARI 1.00): bug, feature_request, performance, billing_problem and other. For template-based categories, the problem wording dominates in both representations.
- Three categories change, and in each case the change follows meaning rather than shared words (details below).
- Silhouettes within categories are lower with BGE (0.21–0.28 vs 0.41–0.54 in notebook 04). That comes from BGE's similarity floor, not from worse themes: theme cohesion stays high (0.87–0.95, section 5).

- **account_access:** BGE groups "I cannot log in; the system says my password is incorrect" with "My account was locked after multiple failed login attempts" (both are password / login failures) and keeps the 2FA problem separate. LSA couldn't group any of the three, because they share no words, so each one was its own theme.
- **security_concern:** BGE puts the vulnerability reports together with "suspicious login" (all possible security incidents) and keeps "encryption and compliance" (a request for information) apart. LSA left suspicious login on its own.
- **how_to:** "Can you explain how to configure data export properly?" moves from the "configure" theme to the "export my data" theme, because it is about data export. Here BGE groups by subject instead of question type. Either grouping is defensible.

title: Notebook 4b: Recurring Issues with Semantic Embeddings: 5. Describe each theme
text:
**22 themes** (notebook 04 had 24). The two largest themes are now the merged ones:
- **login / password failures:** 1,693 tickets, 67% of account_access
- **security incidents** (vulnerabilities + suspicious login): 1,660 tickets, 67% of security_concern

In real data, these would be the first candidates for a permanent fix or a self-service article (for example, a better password-reset flow).

title: Notebook 4b: Recurring Issues with Semantic Embeddings: 6. A 2-D map of the BGE embeddings
text: Categories form clear regions. feature_request and how_to sit next to each other (both are "asking for something"). bug, security_concern, account_access and other share the lower area (problem reports), and performance is its own island. In the right panel, the 7 product versions of each template stay close together, which matches the first table: the problem matters more than the product.

title: Notebook 4b: Recurring Issues with Semantic Embeddings: Summary
text:
| | Notebook 04 (TF-IDF + LSA) | Notebook 4b (BGE) |
|---|---|---|
| What makes sentences similar | shared words | shared meaning, including the same subject (product) |
| Purity with 8 clusters across categories | 0.66 | **0.79** |
| Themes within categories | 24 | 22 |
| Same themes as notebook 04 | – | 5 of 8 categories identical |
| What changed | – | login / password failures merged; security incidents merged; "configure data export" joins the export theme |
| New view | – | 8 subject / intent topics; login area 3,460 tickets across 5 categories, billing area 2,992 |

- The recurring themes from notebook 04 are **confirmed** by a completely different representation, which makes them more trustworthy.
- Where BGE differs, it groups by meaning (login failures, security incidents), which LSA can't do when sentences share no words.
- The cross-category topic view is new: it shows subject areas, such as login and billing, that span several categories.
- The trend over time is not repeated here: the themes are nearly the same, and ticket volumes are flat (notebook 04, section 6).
