The dashboard still reads notebook 04's `clusters.csv`.

title: Notebook 5: Anomaly Detection: Introduction
text:
An anomaly is something that doesn't fit the usual pattern. For a support team, three kinds matter:

| Kind | Question | Method |
|---|---|---|
| **Volume anomaly** | Did a category suddenly get many more (or fewer) tickets than usual? | Compare each period with a rolling baseline (robust z-score) |
| **Hotspot** | Is some group of tickets (a channel, a category, a product) doing much worse than average? | Compare rates with a statistical test |
| **Unusual ticket** | Was a single ticket handled in a strange way? | Isolation Forest |

The robust z-score in one line: `z = (this period's count − usual count) / usual variation`. A z of 3 or more is rare by chance,
so we flag it. "Robust" means we use the median instead of the mean, so one big spike can't hide itself by pulling up the average.

We also **test the detector** by planting fake spikes in a copy of the data. A detector that finds nothing is only useful if we know it *would* have found something.

title: Notebook 5: Anomaly Detection: 1. Volume anomalies
text:
Weekly counts for all tickets (about 95 a week), and monthly counts per category (about 50 a month each; weekly per category would be too small and noisy).
The baseline for each period is the median of the previous 8 periods. We drop the first and last period if they're only partly covered.

### Does the detector actually work? Plant some spikes and see

We copy the weekly series and add extra tickets to random weeks: first +20%, then +40%, and so on. For each size we plant 5 spikes
and count how many the detector catches. This tells us how big a jump has to be before we'd notice it.
We also work out how many flags we'd expect by pure chance at z ≥ 3, to judge whether the real flags mean anything.

**What this tells us**

- The real data has **no weekly spikes** and just **one** flagged category-month (feature_request in March 2025: 70 tickets vs about 44 expected).
  We'd expect about 1.3 flags across all these series purely by chance, so that single flag is consistent with random noise. We report it, but wouldn't sound an alarm on it alone.
- The planted-spike test shows the detector works: it catches every jump of +60% or more, and some jumps of +20–40%.
  With about 95 tickets a week, smaller jumps are hard to tell apart from normal week-to-week variation. More data per period would make the detector more sensitive.

So "no anomalies found" here is a real finding about this (synthetic, very steady) data, not a broken detector.

title: Notebook 5: Anomaly Detection: 2. Hotspots: groups doing worse than average
text:
For each group (each category, channel, region, product, priority...) we compare four rates with the overall rate:

- **negative sentiment**: customer was negative or very negative
- **reopened**: ticket had to be reopened
- **slow resolution**: resolved, but slower than 90% of tickets with the same priority
- **low model confidence**: our classifier wasn't sure (these need manual review)

We use a z-test for proportions. Because we test many groups, some will look unusual by chance, so we also apply a **Bonferroni correction**
(a stricter threshold that accounts for the number of tests).

Eight hotspots survive the strict correction, and they tell two clear stories:

- **Customer frustration:** performance, security_concern, billing_problem and account_access tickets are about 60% negative, against 42% overall.
  These categories need the most attention for customer satisfaction.
- **Model uncertainty:** almost all `other`, `billing_problem`, `account_access` and `security_concern` tickets fall below the confidence threshold.
  That's the classifier struggling with classes it has few sentence types for (notebook 02). Operationally, these are the tickets that will land in manual review,
  so the triage team should expect most of its work from these four categories.

No channel, region, product, platform, segment or SLA plan stands out. Reopen and slow-resolution rates are even across all groups.

title: Notebook 5: Anomaly Detection: 3. Unusual individual tickets: Isolation Forest
text:
Isolation Forest builds many random trees that keep splitting the data. Unusual points get separated (isolated) after only a few splits,
so they get a high anomaly score. We use resolved tickets and five features describing how each one was handled:

- resolution time compared with the usual time for its priority
- priority, reopened or not, sentiment score, CSAT (blank CSAT filled with the middle value 3)

We flag the most unusual 1% and, for each, list the features that make it stand out.

The flagged 1% are mostly **reopened tickets**, often combined with high priority, a negative customer or low CSAT.
Reopening is rare (5% of resolved tickets), so the forest isolates it quickly. That's sensible: a high-priority ticket that was "resolved" and then reopened
by an unhappy customer is exactly the kind of case a team lead should review.

These flagged tickets are actually resolved *faster* than average (21 vs 27 hours). That suggests a "closed too quickly, then reopened" pattern
worth checking in real data.

title: Notebook 5: Anomaly Detection: Summary
text:
| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Weekly volume spikes | None |
| Category-month spikes | 1 (feature_request, March 2025), in line with chance |
| Detector test | Catches all planted jumps of +60% or more |
| Hotspots (Bonferroni-corrected) | Problem categories ~60% negative; four categories mostly low-confidence for the model |
| Unusual tickets (Isolation Forest) | ~100 resolved tickets, mostly reopened, often high priority and unhappy customers |

Saved: `volume_anomalies.csv`, `hotspots.csv`, `ticket_anomalies.csv`, `anomaly_validation.csv` for the dashboard and the GenAI assistant.

title: Notebook 6: GenAI Assistant with RAG: Introduction
text:
The earlier notebooks produced a lot of results: category statistics, two classifiers, SHAP for both, recurring themes, cross-category topics and anomalies.
A support manager shouldn't have to dig through tables to find an answer. So we build an assistant they can ask in plain English,
for example *"Which categories have the most unhappy customers?"* or *"How much does the BGE model reduce manual review?"*

**Why RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)?** A language model on its own doesn't know our data and may confidently make up numbers.
With RAG, we first **retrieve** the most relevant facts from our own results, and then the model **generates** an answer using only those facts.

```
question -> hybrid search over the knowledge base -> top 5 documents -> LLM writes the answer from them -> check the numbers
```

**Design choices**
- **Knowledge base** (about 150 documents), built automatically, with no hand-typed numbers:
  - *data documents* generated from every saved result file (notebooks 01–05 and 02b, 03b, 04b)
  - *narrative documents*: the written interpretation of every notebook section, the evaluation report and the README
- **Retrieval**: hybrid search. TF-IDF keyword similarity is combined with **BGE sentence-embedding** similarity (semantic search), so a question
  finds the right document even when it uses different words. Without `sentence-transformers` it falls back to keywords only.
- **Generation**: **Mistral** (key read from the `.env` file), Claude or any OpenAI-compatible model. If one Mistral model is rate-limited, the next one is tried.
  **Without a key it still works**: an offline mode answers with the most relevant document text.
- **Chat**: follow-up questions are understood, because the previous question is also used for retrieval and the last turns are sent to the LLM.
- **Safety**:
  - the prompt tells the model to use only the given documents
  - sensitive patterns (emails, phone numbers, IP addresses) are masked before anything is sent
  - every number in the answer is checked against the retrieved documents
- The assistant only explains. It never closes or changes tickets, which the brief puts out of scope.

The code lives in `src/rag.py`, so the dashboard uses exactly the same assistant.

title: Notebook 6: GenAI Assistant with RAG: 1. Build the knowledge base
text:
Data documents are generated from the saved result files, and narrative documents from the notebooks and reports.
So if a notebook is re-run with different data, the knowledge base updates automatically.

title: Notebook 6: GenAI Assistant with RAG: 2. Retrieval: does the search find the right document?
text:
Before trusting the answers, we test the search on its own. We wrote **28 questions**, including questions about the embedding models,
SHAP for the BGE model, cross-category topics, the README and the EDA. For each question we list the document (or documents) that answer it.
Some questions are phrased in everyday words on purpose (*"My customers keep getting locked out, what does the data say?"*).

We measure:
- **Hit@1**: how often a right document is the top result
- **Hit@5**: how often one is in the top 5 (the documents passed to the LLM)
- **MRR** (mean reciprocal rank): 1 if always first, 0.5 if always second, and so on

We compare keyword search alone with the hybrid search.

Adding semantic search helps a lot. Hit@1 goes from 61% (keywords only) to **79%**, Hit@5 from 86% to **96%**, and MRR from 0.85 to 0.90.
The biggest gains are on everyday phrasing such as *"My customers keep getting locked out"*, which shares few words with the documents but means the same thing.

Most of the remaining rank-1 misses return a closely related document. For example, *"What are the recurring bug issues?"* returns one specific bug theme first and the full bug theme summary second.
The LLM sees all 5 documents, so the answer is still complete.

### Follow-up questions (chat)

In a chat, people ask short follow-ups like *"and which classes are still weak?"*. We pass the earlier turns as `history`.
The previous question is also used for retrieval, so the follow-up finds the right documents.

Without an API key, the answers come from the best-matching documents word for word, so they're always grounded but can read a bit like a report.
With a key (here Mistral), the LLM writes a shorter, conversational answer from the same documents and cites them in square brackets.

title: Notebook 6: GenAI Assistant with RAG: 4. GenAI + SHAP: explain a single prediction
text:
For a new ticket, we combine three things: the model's prediction, the SHAP words that drove it (notebook 03),
and the retrieved facts about that category. The assistant turns them into a short explanation for the support agent.
The dashboard does the same with the BGE model and its word-level SHAP (notebook 3b).

title: Notebook 6: GenAI Assistant with RAG: 5. The grounding check
text:
Every number in an answer must appear in the documents the assistant was given. Here's what happens with an honest answer and with a made-up one:

The invented "75%" isn't in the source, so the answer is flagged. The dashboard shows a warning next to any answer that fails this check.

title: Notebook 6: GenAI Assistant with RAG: Summary
text:
| Part | What we did | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Knowledge base | ~150 documents: data documents from every saved result, plus the written interpretation of every notebook section, the evaluation report and the README | Updates automatically when results change |
| Retrieval | Hybrid: TF-IDF keywords + BGE semantic search | Right document first for 79% of 28 test questions, in the top 5 for 96% |
| Generation | Mistral (from `.env`) with automatic fallback between models; Claude / OpenAI-compatible also supported; offline mode | Always answers, even without internet |
| Chat | Follow-up questions use the earlier turns | Short follow-ups find the right documents |
| Explainability | SHAP words + retrieved category facts | Plain-English reason for each prediction |
| Safety | Masking, context-only prompt, number check | Made-up numbers are caught |

**To use an LLM:** put the Mistral key in `.env` (either `MISTRAL_API_KEY=...` or just the key on one line), or set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` / `OPENAI_API_KEY`.
Model names are in `src/config.py`.

title: Evaluation report: 1. Data and class distribution
text:
- Stratified sample of **20,000** tickets from a synthetic dataset of 100,000 (seed 42); category shares match the full data.
- **8 categories**, balanced: largest how_to 12.7%, smallest bug 12.3% (imbalance ratio 1.03). No resampling needed.
- Only **96 unique messages**; each always carries the same label. account_access, billing_problem and other have just 3 sentences each.
- Cleaning: `csat_score = 0` → not rated; missing region → "Unknown"; resolution fields left empty for unfinished tickets.
- Figures: `01_target.png`, `06_class_balance.png`.

title: Evaluation report: 2. Split strategy and leakage
text:
| Issue | Decision |
|---|---|
| Same 96 sentences repeat across tickets | **Split by message**: test sentences are never seen in training. A random split gives a misleading macro F1 of 1.00. |
| `agent_first_reply`, `resolution_summary` map one-to-one to the label | Excluded from model inputs |
| Status, sentiment, CSAT, resolution time are known only after handling | Excluded from model inputs; used in analytics only |

Hold-out test: 20% of messages per category (4,523 tickets from 20 messages). Stability check: grouped 5-fold cross-validation.

title: Evaluation report: 3. Baseline and model comparison
text:
Test set (unseen messages):

| Model | Accuracy | Macro precision | Macro recall | Macro F1 | Weighted F1 | Macro ROC-AUC |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Majority baseline | 0.049 | 0.006 | 0.125 | 0.012 | 0.005 | 0.500 |
| Naive Bayes | 0.630 | 0.573 | 0.750 | 0.611 | 0.548 | 0.915 |
| Linear SVM | 0.630 | 0.573 | 0.750 | 0.611 | 0.548 | 0.886 |
| Logistic Regression | 0.630 | 0.573 | 0.750 | 0.611 | 0.548 | 0.886 |

Grouped 5-fold CV macro F1: 0.591 ± 0.051 for all three real models (baseline 0.002).
**Chosen: Logistic Regression.** It ties on F1, gives probabilities for the confidence score, and its SHAP values are exact.

title: Evaluation report: 4. Final model: per-class results (out-of-fold, all 20,000 tickets)
text:
| Category | Precision | Recall | F1 | ROC-AUC |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| account_access | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.65 |
| billing_problem | 0.50 | 0.34 | 0.41 | 0.89 |
| bug | 0.75 | 1.00 | 0.86 | 1.00 |
| feature_request | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| how_to | 0.51 | 1.00 | 0.67 | 1.00 |
| other | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.00 | 0.64 |
| performance | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| security_concern | 0.49 | 0.33 | 0.40 | 0.72 |
| **Macro average** | **0.53** | **0.58** | **0.54** | **0.86** |
| **Weighted average** | 0.53 | 0.58 | 0.54 | |

Accuracy 0.585. **Minority categories:** the three 3-sentence classes are the weakest (account_access and other F1 0.00, billing_problem 0.41).

title: Evaluation report: 5. Confusion and error analysis
text:
Most frequent confusions (out-of-fold):

| Actual → Predicted | Tickets | Why |
|---|---|---|
| other → how_to | 1,659 | "I need help but I'm not sure..." looks like "I need help setting up..." |
| account_access → security_concern | 863 | "account was locked after failed **login** attempts" vs "suspicious **login** on my account" |
| security_concern → other | 832 | "We need details about your data encryption" shares "need", "details" with vague requests |
| account_access → billing_problem / bug | 830 / 829 | Unseen password and 2FA wording shares few words with the other access sentences |
| billing_problem → how_to / account_access | 821 / 814 | Unseen billing wording ("downgraded my plan", "invoice") |

The model matches words rather than meaning. With so few sentences per class, unseen wording in small classes is easily confused. Figure: `22_confusion_matrix.png`.

title: Evaluation report: 6. Low-confidence handling
text:
- Rule: confidence below **60%** → Manual Triage queue.
- 45.7% of tickets fall below the threshold (out-of-fold).
- **Auto-routed tickets are 92% correct; reviewed tickets only 18%**, so the rule catches most mistakes.
- Confidence is only partly calibrated (e.g. some correct billing predictions sit below 40%), so the threshold should be tuned on real data. The dashboard has a slider for this.
- Figure: `24_confidence.png`.

title: Evaluation report: 7. Worked examples (model trained on training messages only)
text:
| Case | Message | Prediction | Confidence | Decision |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Common (seen) | "I need help setting up data export for my team." | how_to | 0.99 | Auto-route to Service Desk (L1) |
| Ambiguous | "The billing page is very slow and keeps showing an error." | performance (runner-up bug) | 0.71 | Auto-route to Platform / SRE |
| Minority class, new wording | "My account was locked after multiple failed login attempts." | security_concern | 0.47 | Manual review |
| Out of scope | "The coffee machine on the third floor is broken." | bug | 0.46 | Manual review |

title: Evaluation report: 8. Explainability
text:
Exact SHAP values for the linear model (verified to add up to the model's scores). Key words per class are sensible
(e.g. "charged twice", "subscription" → billing; "timing out", "queries" → performance; "suspicious", "vulnerability" → security).
Filler words ("my", "the", "after") also carry weight because of template sentences. Figures: `30–32_shap_*.png`.

title: Evaluation report: 9. Recurring issues and anomalies (summary)
text:
- **24 recurring themes** from text embeddings + K-Means within categories, e.g. pages crashing, changes not saving, queries timing out. Themes are coherent (cohesion 0.76–1.00).
- **Volume:** no weekly spikes; 1 category-month flag (in line with chance). The detector catches every planted spike of +60% or more.
- **Hotspots:** performance, security_concern, billing_problem and account_access are about 60% negative vs 42% overall.
- **Unusual tickets:** 102 resolved tickets flagged by Isolation Forest, mostly reopened, often high priority.

title: Evaluation report: 10. Limitations
text:
- Synthetic data: generated labels and timestamps, even distributions, hard resolution-time limits per priority.
- Only 96 unique sentences, so the scores measure generalisation to new wording on very little variety. Real data should score higher.
- The routing table (category → queue) is assumed; the data has no assignment group.
- TF-IDF matches words, not meaning; sentence embeddings or more varied training text are the main improvements.
- The GenAI assistant uses keyword retrieval; LLM answers need an API key (offline mode otherwise).

title: Project README: Introduction
text:
HCLTech Future Ready Data Science Hackathon · Use case 4

Support teams receive thousands of tickets and sort them by hand, which slows down routing and hides problems that keep coming back.
This project reads a ticket's description, predicts its category with a confidence score, sends uncertain tickets to a person,
finds recurring issues and anomalies, and puts it all in a dashboard with a GenAI assistant you can ask questions in plain English.

title: Project README: How to run
text:
```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt

jupyter nbconvert --to notebook --execute --inplace notebooks/0*.ipynb

streamlit run app.py
```

The zip already contains all outputs, so you can start the dashboard straight away (step 3).
If the dashboard can't load the model (a scikit-learn version difference), just re-run notebook 02 once.

**Optional: real LLM answers.** Without a key, the assistant works offline. To use an LLM, set one of these before starting Jupyter or Streamlit:

```bash
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...        # Claude
```

title: Project README: Key results
text:
| Area | Result |
|---|---|
| Data | 20,000 tickets, 8 balanced categories (ratio 1.03), only 96 unique messages |
| Leakage | Random split gives a misleading macro F1 of 1.00. We split by message instead. `agent_first_reply` and `resolution_summary` give away the label and are excluded. |
| Model comparison | LR, SVM and Naive Bayes tie on macro F1 (0.59 in grouped CV); LR chosen for probabilities and exact SHAP |
| Final model (out-of-fold) | Macro F1 0.54, weighted F1 0.54, macro ROC-AUC 0.86 |
| Semantic embeddings (02b) | BGE + LR / SVM reach macro F1 0.81–0.82 in grouped CV vs 0.59 for TF-IDF; account_access 0.00 → 0.80, manual review 46% → 17% |
| Strong / weak classes | bug, feature_request, how_to, performance near perfect on new wording; account_access and other fail (3 sentences each) |
| Low confidence | Below 60% → manual review (46% of tickets). Auto-routed tickets are 92% correct; reviewed ones only 18%, so the rule catches most mistakes |
| SHAP | Sensible key words per class, plus filler words caused by template sentences (a stated limitation) |
| SHAP for embeddings (03b) | Key words in every category's top 3 (password, error, suspicious…); deleting the top SHAP word hurts the prediction 5× more than a random word; stop-word share similar to TF-IDF (26% vs 27%) |
| Recurring issues | 24 coherent themes (e.g. pages crashing, changes not saving, queries timing out) |
| Clustering with embeddings (04b) | 5 of 8 categories get the same themes as notebook 04; BGE merges login/password failures and security incidents; a new topic view shows a login area of 3,460 tickets across 5 categories |
| Anomalies | No real volume spikes (detector catches every planted spike of +60% or more); problem categories ~60% negative vs 42% overall |
| GenAI | Right source document in the top 4 for all 13 test questions; invented numbers are flagged |

**Why the scores look modest:** the test only contains wording the model has never seen, and the dataset has very few
different sentences per category. This is the honest number. The commonly reported ~100% comes from the same sentences appearing in training and test.

title: Project README: Assumptions and limitations
text:
- The data is a synthetic Kaggle dataset. Labels come from its `issue_type` column and timestamps are generated.
- There is no assignment-group column, so the category → support queue table in `src/config.py` is our own assumption.
- `csat_score = 0` is treated as "not rated".
- Only 96 different messages exist, so the classifier is tested on a hard task: new wording. Real, more varied data would likely score higher.
- Notebooks 02b, 03b and 04b need `pip install sentence-transformers` and download three models (~0.6 GB) the first time. The dashboard still uses the TF-IDF model, SHAP and themes from notebooks 02–04, so it doesn't need PyTorch.
- Text embeddings in notebook 04 use TF-IDF + LSA so everything runs offline. Notebook 04 has a switch for `sentence-transformers` if it's installed.
- The `shap` library is optional: SHAP values for the linear model are computed exactly with the same formula `shap.LinearExplainer` uses, and notebook 03 cross-checks against the library if it's installed.
- The system suggests categories and routing and explains results; it never closes or changes tickets.
